messages.content: Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

output:
## We started pairing juniors with seniors, and I got the design wrong twice

The first version was a spreadsheet. Eight mentor/mentee pairs, matched by tech stack, meet every other week. By week six, four pairs had quietly stopped meeting and nobody wanted to say so out loud.

Here's what broke it: I never told anyone what the meetings were *for*. "Career growth" is not an agenda. Two people sit down, one of them is supposed to be wise, and the whole thing collapses into a status update with extra guilt.

The second version failed differently. I over-specified — a topic guide, a reading list, a shared doc template. People filled out the template instead of talking.

What finally stuck is smaller than either. Each pair picks one real thing the mentee is stuck on. A gnarly service they can't reason about, a review they keep getting torn apart on, the promo packet they've rewritten four times. That's the whole scope. When it's done, the pairing ends, and they can re-up or not.

Three details that mattered more than I expected. Mentors get an hour a week of protected time, on the calendar, defended by their manager — otherwise it's unpaid emotional labor and the good ones burn out first. Mentees choose their mentor; assignment killed it last time. And no pair reports to each other, ever.

We're six months in. Nine active pairs out of a team of thirty-four, two people promoted who credit it, one pair that ended after three weeks because the mentee got what she needed and said so.

That last one is the success case, not the failure.
